1:
What kind of psalm this is the commentators settle first. Calvin calls it a common prayer of the Church on behalf of the King of Israel, that God would succour him in danger and maintain his kingdom, since in David's person the well-being of the whole community centred. Clarke gives the argument by sections — a prayer for the king in his enterprises, confidence of victory expressed, vain hopes exposed and supplication renewed — and calls it one of the dialogue psalms, likely penned when David went to war with the Ammonites and Syrians. Keil and Delitzsch place it between its neighbours: it follows the psalm before because its opening echoes the prayer that closes it, and pairs with the psalm after as intercession pairs with thanksgiving, both closing with an ejaculatory cry to Jahve. Henry notices the propriety of David's writing a form of prayer for the congregation to use on his behalf: those who desire their friends' prayers should tell them particularly what to ask, and even great and good men, who know well how to pray for themselves, must earnestly desire the prayers of others, as Paul often begged of his friends.

On the day of trouble the readings run from the historical to the devotional. Ellicott hears the patriarch behind the phrase, since the God of Jacob recalls Jacob's own words about the God who answered him in the day of his distress, and observes that the name alone of that God was a safeguard to the people called after their forefather. Wesley says only that God had made a covenant with Jacob and his posterity. Henry draws two notes from the phrase: that even the greatest of men may be much in trouble, since neither the crown on David's head nor the grace in his heart exempted him, and must be much in prayer, since David, a man of business and of war, did not think the prayers of his prophets and priests excused him from praying for himself — the prayers of others being desired not to supersede but to second our own.

Gill and Spurgeon read the whole psalm of Christ, and the day of trouble of his days. All Christ's days were days of trouble, Gill says: a brother born for adversity, a man of sorrows, persecuted by Herod in his infancy, tempted by Satan in the wilderness, harassed by the Scribes and Pharisees, grieved at the unbelief of that generation and sometimes made uneasy by his own disciples — though the day of trouble was above all the garden, where his sweat was as it were great drops of blood, and the cross. Spurgeon puts it as the church's answering intercession: the Saviour's days of trouble were also his days of prayer, so the church joins her intercession with her Lord's and pleads that he be heard in his cries and tears — the agony in the garden being the gloomiest hour, where he was heard in that he feared.

Augustine reads the psalm as prophecy addressed to Christ, the prophet speaking to him under the form of a wish and foretelling things to come. The Lord hear thee in the day of trouble is the day in which he said, Father, glorify thy Son; the name of the God of Jacob protects him because to him belongs the younger people, since the elder shall serve the younger. Help sent from the sanctuary is the making of a sanctified body, the Church; the remembrance of his sacrifice is a prayer that we be made mindful of all the injuries he bore for us; and the burnt offering made fat is the turning of the cross, whereon he was wholly offered up to God, into the joy of the resurrection.
2:
Where the help is to come from is the first question. Gill allows two senses for the sanctuary — either the tabernacle, the holy place where the ark stood as the symbol of the divine presence, or heaven, the habitation of God's holiness — though he inclines to take it as the same thing meant by Zion in the clause that follows, the church of God, from which he sends the rod of his strength. Wesley keeps it concrete: the tabernacle in Zion, where the ark then was, and toward which the Israelites directed their prayers. Clarke takes both clauses together and reads them forward. The sanctuary was the place where God recorded his name, where he was to be sought and where he manifested himself, dwelling between the cherubim over the mercy-seat; and he is now in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, so that this is the true sanctuary where God must be sought. Zion he glosses as the temple or tabernacle where the prayers and sacrifices were to be offered.

Keil and Delitzsch read the psalm as liturgy rather than as a text, and set these verses in the action they accompany: while they were being sung the offering of the sacrifice was probably going on, and after a lengthened pause a voice — probably that of one of the Levites — rises to express the cheering assurance that the offering presented by the priest has been graciously accepted. The word that opens the later verse is the usual one marking a turning-point, the instantaneous entrance of a result after some prolonged process, whether hidden or manifest; and the verb that follows it they call a perfect of faith, which in the certainty of being answered realises the fulfilment before it comes.

The offerings themselves Clarke and Ellicott distinguish by kind. Clarke notes that the minchah named here was a gratitude-offering, rarely used of a bloody sacrifice, while the olah was a bloody one, the blood of the victim spilt at the altar and the flesh consumed; the one implied a consciousness of sin and was brought as an atonement, the other a sense of mercies already received and was offered in the way of gratitude — and David presents himself with offerings of both kinds. Ellicott sets the scene from the custom, the king sacrificing before battle, and offers a rendering of his own. Since the word elsewhere translated memorial, a derivative of the verb here rendered remember, has been shown by eminent scholars to signify incense, he thinks the psalmist meant accept the incense of all thy minchah and the fat of thy olah — one scholar going so far as to render the two verbs smell and relish. Accept he takes literally as make fat, that is, regard or receive as a worthy offering, and he rejects the alternative rendering turn to ashes on the ground that the Hebrew word never elsewhere bears that sense but only that of cleansing from ashes.

Of the grant according to the heart the two notes go different ways. Clarke supposes the words the high priest's prayer, that God would give the king whatever he was setting his heart upon and accomplish all his desires. Gill reads them of Christ, whose own heart's desire is to see his seed and the travail of his soul, to have the pleasure of the Lord prosper in his hand, and to have all his people called, preserved and glorified. Clarke adds a word on the Selah that closes the people's prayer, which he takes in the general sense of so be it — hear and answer; it will and must be so.
5:
The verse is the congregation's resolve, and Gill reads the salvation it rejoices in two ways. It may be the salvation the Messiah himself is possessed of, his deliverance from death and the grave and every other enemy — not his sufferings and death only but chiefly his resurrection, his session at God's right hand and his intercession, which cause the triumph of faith and further its joy; or it may be the salvation he is the author of, so great and so suitable, so complete and everlasting, that it is matter of joy to all who are sensible of their need of it and have a comfortable hope of interest in it. Wesley takes the whole line as a display of confidence and an assurance of the victory, the name invoked to the honour of God and the banners set up by way of triumph.

Spurgeon presses the tense. In Jesus there is salvation; it is his own, and hence called thy salvation, but ours to receive and ours to rejoice in — and we should fixedly resolve that come what may we will rejoice in the saving arm of the Lord Jesus. The people in this psalm felt sure of victory before their king went to battle and began rejoicing beforehand; how much more ought we, who have seen the victory completely won. Unbelief begins weeping for the funeral before the man is dead, he says; why should not faith commence piping before the dance of victory begins? Buds are beautiful, and promises not yet fulfilled are worthy to be admired. If joy were more general among the Lord's people God would be more glorified among men, since the happiness of the subjects is the honour of the sovereign.

On the banners the readings are practical and then martial. Ellicott corrects the verb — rather, we will wave our banners — and pictures the whole army, or their representatives, assembled in the Temple courts and raising the encouraging shout. Clarke takes the words as spoken by David and his officers: we expect help from thee alone, it is in thy cause we engage, and to thee, our war being a just one, we consecrate our banners, inscribed with thy name. He adds the etymology that hangs on such an inscription, that the Maccabees are said to have taken their name from the words on their standards, drawn from the song at the sea — who is like unto thee, O Lord, among the gods — the initial letters of which give the name Maccabeus. After the officers' words, he supposes, the high priest added the closing petition, that the Lord fulfil all thy requests.

Spurgeon takes the same banner as a standing posture rather than a single occasion. We lift the standard of defiance in the face of the foe and wave the flag of victory over the fallen adversary; some proclaim war in the name of one king and some of another, but the faithful go to war in Jesus' name, the name of the incarnate God, Immanuel, God with us. The times are evil at present, he grants, but so long as Jesus lives and reigns in his church we need not furl our banners in fear but may advance them with sacred courage — and he quotes the verse that says it for him, that the tremendous name of Jesus puts all our foes to flight, and that the meek and angry Lamb is a lion in the fight. The church cannot forget that Jesus is her advocate before the throne, and so sums up all the desires already expressed in the one short sentence with which the verse closes.
6:
Who the anointed is divides them at once. Gill denies it is David — though David was the anointed of the God of Jacob and anointed with material oil by Samuel at God's express order — and takes the whole verse of the Messiah, anointed king over the holy hill of Zion with the oil of gladness; the church, rising in her faith, is strongly assured that though his troubles would be many and great he should be delivered out of them all, freed from the sorrows of death, raised from the dead, given all power in heaven and earth, and that all the members of his body should be saved through him, which is in a sense the salvation of himself. Ellicott takes the opposite view and states it as a rule of reading: better, now know I that Jehovah hath saved his anointed, meaning the king who is the subject of the poem, since it is out of keeping with the rest of the psalm to understand Israel or an ideal king here.

What the now marks they agree on. Ellicott calls it emphatic — the confidence expressed after the sacrifice has been seen performed and felt to be accepted — and Clarke supposes these the words of the priest after the victim had been consumed and the signs of acceptance had appeared, so that the campaign might be counted on to have a successful issue. Clarke adds the caution that keeps the assurance from presumption: David is God's anointed and therefore under his especial care, but he must continue to pray and to depend on God, else he cannot expect continual salvation, and having vast multitudes of enemies against him he requires supernatural help. He then parses the closing phrase by degrees — the hand of God is his power, the right hand his almighty power, the strength of the right hand that power in action. Wesley reads the tense as certainty rather than sequence: they are already sure of victory from the consideration of God's power and faithfulness and love, and they speak as one person because they were unanimous in the prayer.

Ellicott marks a shift between this verse and the prayer that opened the psalm. There the sanctuary had been named as the residence of the divine power, with the ark deposited in it as its symbol; here the inspiration expresses a higher conviction, that the manifestation of succour will come not through any earthly symbol of God's might but immediately from his dwelling-place on high.

Henry finds the ground of the assurance in the praying rather than the sacrifice. David — or the psalmist who penned it — knows the Lord saves his anointed because God has stirred up the hearts of the seed of Jacob to pray for him; and it bodes well to any prince and people, and may justly be taken as a happy presage, when God pours upon them a spirit of prayer, since if he sees us seeking him he will be found of us, and if he causes us to hope in his word he will establish his word to us. The answer, Henry says, takes its rise from above, since God hears from his holy heaven, of which the sanctuary was a type, and from the throne prepared there, of which the mercy-seat was a type; and it takes effect below, since he hears with the saving strength of his right hand — a real answer, not by letter nor by word of mouth but by what he does, making it appear that he hears by what he performs.
7:
The contrast turns on a verb our version supplies, which Clarke and Ellicott both want out. Clarke calls the original short and emphatic — these in chariots, and these in horses, but we will record in the name of Jehovah our God — the Greek having we shall be magnified and the Latin we shall invoke the name of the Lord. Ellicott says the poetry is weakened by inserting the word trust, and renders it these in chariots and these on horses, but we in the name of Jehovah our God make boast. Wesley glosses remember in a word: trust. Both read the mention of cavalry as dating the psalm — Clarke to the war with the Ammonites and Syrians, who came with vast multitudes of horsemen and chariots, Ellicott to a Syrian war, the armies of Syria being peculiarly strong in that arm. Clarke adds the disadvantage that made the boast necessary: by the law David could have neither chariots nor horses, so those who came against him with cavalry had a great advantage — but he saw that Jehovah was more than a match for all his foes.

Gill fills in what such an army could do, then turns the verse inward. Chariots were useful for carriage and terrible in battle, and he instances the currus falcati with scythes at their sides, which driven among infantry cut them down as grass is mown; war-horses do execution by pawing and trampling. Yet these are vain things for safety, since salvation and victory are of the Lord — as are the chariots and horses of the sun and the idols the Gentiles trusted in, and all the external things men depend on for salvation: fleshly privileges, outward works, morality, a profession of religion, a round of duties, all disclaimed by those who know the way of life by Christ.

On the reversal that follows they agree, and one of them stages it. Gill has those who rode and trusted brought down from their places of honour and falling to the ground by death, and adds the parallel of those who, lifted to heaven like Capernaum with their own attainments, are brought down to hell. Clarke says they were so confident of victory that they looked on it as already gained, and are now bowed down and prostrated, while those who trusted in the name are raised from all despondency and stand upright — we shall conquer, and go on to conquer. Wesley has them brought down from the horses and chariots they trusted, and the others standing firmly and keeping the field. Ellicott sees a whole battle fought before our eyes: those formerly struck down rise, return to the fight, beat off their foes and in their turn lay them low.

Spurgeon reads the two ends as a comment on two foundations. The enemies of God are uppermost at first, but before long are brought down by force or fall of their own accord, since their foundation is rotten and gives way — their chariots burned, their horses dead of pestilence, and where is their boasted strength? Those who rest on Jehovah are often cast down at the first onset, but an Almighty arm uplifts them and they joyfully stand upright; the victory of Jesus is the inheritance of his people, and the world, death, Satan and sin shall all be trampled beneath the feet of faith's champions. He carries the thought into the psalm's close, which he takes as a recapitulation: that Jesus might himself be delivered, and might then as our King hear us, is its twofold desire — the first request granted, the second sure to all the seed. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same close as staging: after the solo voice the chorus comes on again, so that the song is closed as it was opened, by the whole congregation, recurring to its primary note.
9:
Everything in the last line turns on where the pause falls, and each witness stakes out a position. Gill rejects the Greek, Ethiopic and Arabic punctuation that pulls the word king up into the opening cry, Aben Ezra's objection being decisive for him — the accent separates those words from what follows. He would rather supply us, as the Syriac does with the Lord will deliver us, and the Targum with redeem us. Divided so, the first petition addresses Jehovah the Father and the second the King Messiah, and the deliverance begged is temporal, spiritual and eternal together.

Ellicott argues the other way and weighs what each arrangement costs. Our translators followed the Masoretic accentuation, but at the price of spoiling the rhythm and interrupting the sense; the Septuagint and Vulgate, with every modern commentator after them, break the line elsewhere and give Jehovah, save the king — whence, he observes, our National Anthem. That arrangement makes Jehovah the subject of the closing verb, may he hear us in the day of our calling; and the slide from second person into third he counts characteristic of the Hebrew way of mastering emotion, letting a poem die away at the end in calm and subdued language.

Clarke lays the versions side by side before choosing among them on other grounds. The words were sung by the whole congregation as the chorus and conclusion of the piece, and may run Lord, save the king — he will hear as in the day of our calling. Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, Arabic and Anglo-Saxon agree on Lord, save the king, and hear us whensoever we shall call upon thee, which refers everything to God; the Syriac stands apart with the Lord will save us, and our king will hear us in the day in which we shall call upon him, which hands the second half to David. Clarke prefers the Syriac as the easiest sense and the one harmonising with all the rest — save David, and David will save us; preserve him, and he will be thy minister for good to us. Wesley cuts through the whole dispute by identifying the king with God himself, the supreme monarch, the king of kings, and in a peculiar manner the king of Israel — on which reading the congregation is not praying for its sovereign at all, but asking the one true Sovereign to answer them when they call.
